item.text: The evidence is converging around a mixed 2022 record: concrete federal expansions and implementation in coverage, veterans’ care, water infrastructure, and rental aid; measurable recovery in mortality; but sharp deterioration in child poverty, food security, educational achievement, and persistent affordability/racial gaps. I’m now checking the underlying pages and separating 2022 delivery from laws whose benefits began later.

## Research scope

Target: Joe Biden, United States, calendar year 2022  
Chapter: 6B — Social Well-Being and Human Development  
Purpose: reusable evidence dossier only; no score assigned.

The United States entered 2022 with high aggregate human-development capacity but entrenched racial, income, geographic, health-access, housing, and educational inequalities. Biden exercised substantial authority over federal agencies and implementation, but Congress controlled legislation and appropriations, while states and localities administered education, Medicaid, public health, housing assistance, and much social-service delivery. Pandemic recovery, inflation, supply-chain disruption, Federal Reserve policy, and state decisions materially affected outcomes.

## Fully extracted evidence

### WEB-6B-001 — Expiration of pandemic tax relief sharply increased child poverty

The Supplemental Poverty Measure rose from 7.8% in 2021 to 12.4% in 2022. More than five million additional children were in SPM poverty after stimulus payments and expanded refundable tax credits—including the temporary expanded Child Tax Credit—expired. In 2021, pandemic-era tax provisions had removed 7.3 million children from poverty; that protection was not continued for 2022.

This is strong evidence that a major, demonstrably effective child-welfare intervention was not made durable. Biden publicly supported extending the expanded CTC, but Congress did not enact the extension; responsibility is therefore shared and cannot be assigned solely to the executive. Inflation also raised household needs.

Strongest source: “Poverty Measure That Includes Government Assistance Increased to 12.4% in 2022, When Pandemic Relief Ended,” U.S. Census Bureau, September 12, 2023, lines 203–215. [Direct source](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2023/09/supplemental-poverty-measure.html)

Caution: In July 2026, Census announced that BLS had found errors in SPM thresholds and that revised 2019–2024 estimates would be issued. The reported 2022 levels should therefore be treated as provisional pending those revisions, although the expiration of the tax provisions is not in dispute.

Lenses: 6B.1, 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.6, 6B.9, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-002 — Food insecurity worsened broadly in 2022

USDA’s nationally representative Food Security Supplement found that 12.8% of households—17.0 million—experienced food insecurity in 2022, up significantly from 10.2% in 2021. Very low food security rose from 3.8% to 5.1%. Food insecurity among households with children rose from 12.5% to 17.3%; children themselves experienced food insecurity in 8.8% of households with children, up from 6.2%. In 381,000 households, children sometimes went hungry, skipped meals, or did not eat for a whole day for lack of money.

This is a direct target-year welfare outcome and important contrary evidence to claims of broadly improved life chances. USDA expressly does not assign causes: inflation, household circumstances, and federal, state, and local policies all mattered. Continued nutrition benefits mitigated hardship—55% of food-insecure households reported recent participation in SNAP, WIC, or school meals—but did not prevent deterioration.

Strongest source: Rabbitt et al., “Household Food Security in the United States in 2022,” USDA Economic Research Service, October 25, 2023, report ERR-325, summary pp. 5–6 and pp. 22–23. [Direct report](https://www.ers.usda.gov/sites/default/files/_laserfiche/publications/107703/ERR-325.pdf?v=24727)

Caution: The survey instrument was revised in 2022, but USDA states that the underlying measurement methodology remained unchanged and the headline series remains comparable.

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-003 — Health-insurance coverage reached a historic high

CMS recorded 14.5 million Marketplace plan selections or automatic reenrollments for 2022, including 3.0 million new consumers. HHS’s National Health Interview Survey analysis estimated that the uninsured rate reached a historic low of 8.0% in the first quarter of 2022, with 5.2 million people gaining coverage since 2020.

The American Rescue Plan’s enhanced premium subsidies, an extended enrollment period, and federal outreach are meaningfully attributable to Biden and his administration, although the ACA infrastructure was inherited and state-based marketplaces administered part of the enrollment. This is strong evidence of delivered improvement in formal access and affordability, not merely an announcement.

Strongest sources: “Marketplace 2022 Open Enrollment Period Report: Final National Snapshot,” CMS, January 27, 2022, lines 62–63. [CMS enrollment report](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/marketplace-2022-open-enrollment-period-report-final-national-snapshot); “National Uninsured Rate Reaches All-Time Low in Early 2022,” HHS/ASPE, August 2, 2022. [ASPE report](https://aspe.hhs.gov/reports/2022-uninsurance-at-all-time-low)

Limitation: Plan selection is not identical to effectuated or continuous coverage, and insurance does not establish affordable access to actual care.

Lenses: 6B.1, 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-004 — Insurance gains did not eliminate severe affordability barriers

The Commonwealth Fund’s 2022 survey found that 46% of working-age respondents had skipped or delayed care because of cost, while 42% had medical-bill or medical-debt problems. Forty-nine percent could not pay an unexpected $1,000 medical bill within 30 days; the figure was 68% among adults with low income, 69% among Black adults, and 63% among Hispanic adults.

This independently limits the significance of the coverage gains: formal insurance expanded, but underinsurance and unequal financial exposure remained widespread. The survey reflects the structure of employer, Marketplace, Medicaid, and state health systems accumulated over many administrations; it is weak evidence of a uniquely Biden-caused failure but strong evidence about the actual welfare baseline and unresolved distributional gaps.

Strongest source: “The State of U.S. Health Insurance in 2022,” Commonwealth Fund, September 29, 2022, lines 150–155, 196–197 and 255. [Direct source](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/issue-briefs/2022/sep/state-us-health-insurance-2022-biennial-survey)

Caution: Survey answers are self-reported; subgroup estimates should be read with the report’s sampling methodology and confidence intervals.

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-005 — Inflation Reduction Act created durable health-cost institutions, mostly effective after 2022

Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act on August 16, 2022. It extended enhanced ACA premium assistance and established durable changes to Medicare drug policy: $35 monthly cost sharing for covered insulin and no cost sharing for recommended adult vaccines from 2023, elimination of catastrophic-phase cost sharing in 2024, a $2,000 Part D annual out-of-pocket cap in 2025, expanded low-income subsidies, inflation rebates, and Medicare drug-price negotiation.

This is strong ruler-attributed institutional evidence because Biden advocated for and signed the legislation and CMS began implementation. It is not a 2022 realized-outcome record: most beneficiary savings began in 2023 or later. Congressional enactment and earlier legislative efforts deserve substantial shared attribution.

Strongest source: “Reduced Drug Prices, Enhanced Medicare Benefits Under the Inflation Reduction Act: Frequently Asked Questions,” CMS, October 5, 2022, pp. 1–2, lines 18–55. [Direct CMS document](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/10522-external-faqs-about-inflation-reduction-act.pdf)

Contrary evidence: The enacted insulin cap applied to Medicare, not all privately insured or uninsured insulin users; later benefits cannot be counted as 2022 delivery.

Lenses: 6B.1, 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.9, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-006 — PACT Act expanded veterans’ health and disability protection

Biden signed the bipartisan PACT Act on August 10, 2022. Beginning October 1, VA expanded health-care eligibility for specified Vietnam-era, Gulf War, and post-9/11 veterans exposed to toxic hazards. The law added presumptive conditions, required toxic-exposure screening, and supported research and workforce capacity. This reduced the evidentiary burden formerly placed on sick veterans to prove individual causation.

The legislation directly addressed a vulnerable, previously underserved group and created durable statutory entitlements and administrative systems. Attribution is strong but shared with Congress and veterans’ advocates. Initial eligibility expansion occurred in 2022; the bulk of applications, screenings, and health outcomes accrued later.

Strongest source: “VA opens health care eligibility for Vietnam, Gulf War, post-9/11 Veterans under PACT Act,” Department of Veterans Affairs, September 28, 2022, lines 62–73. [Direct source](https://news.va.gov/press-room/va-opens-health-care-eligibility-for-vietnam-gulf-war-post-9-11-veterans-under-pact-act/)

Later corroboration: VA reported in March 2023 that more than 360,000 veterans and survivors had applied, 2.1 million veterans had received exposure screening, and more than 185,000 had enrolled in VA care. These figures are implementation evidence, not 2022 outcomes.

Lenses: 6B.1, 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.8, 6B.9, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-007 — Federal water investment moved from authorization into awards

EPA’s first-year Bipartisan Infrastructure Law report recorded approximately $9.10 billion in FY2022 water appropriations and $4.24 billion obligated by November 1, 2022. That included approximately $1.17 billion obligated for drinking-water lead-service-line replacement and $1.17 billion in general drinking-water revolving funds. EPA reported awarding the first 20 state capitalization grants for lead-line identification and replacement and required funded programs to develop strategies intended to direct at least 40% of benefits to disadvantaged communities.

This is meaningful implementation toward durable basic infrastructure rather than a pledge alone. Biden advocated for and signed the 2021 law and EPA administered it in 2022, but Congress supplied the statute and states and utilities determine project execution. Obligations are not completed pipe replacements or demonstrated 2022 health outcomes.

Strongest source: “Bipartisan Infrastructure Law: EPA’s Year One Anniversary Report,” EPA, November 2022, funding table. [Direct report](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-11/V-4_BIL_FirstAnniversaryReport_Nov142022.pdf)

Caution: EPA is both implementer and reporter; completed-project and distributional evidence is needed before inferring broad realized access gains.

Lenses: 6B.1, 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.8, 6B.9.

### WEB-6B-008 — Rental aid prevented evictions but suffered serious delivery and oversight weaknesses

GAO found that the $46.55 billion Emergency Rental Assistance program helped low-income renters and likely limited evictions. In available data, 85% of ERA1 recipient households had income below 50% of area median. Treasury introduced self-attestation and reallocated approximately $3.1 billion by October 2022 to accelerate access.

However, about one-quarter of grantees had made no payments five months into the program; incomplete recipient data covered roughly 26% of 2021 household payments; and Treasury’s reallocation did not consistently align resources with renter need or grantee capacity. GAO found inadequate risk assessment and monitoring.

ERA1 originated in the December 2020 legislation preceding Biden; ERA2 was enacted through Biden’s 2021 American Rescue Plan. Biden-era Treasury receives material credit for administrative flexibilities and reallocation, but delivery depended on more than 700 state, local, territorial, and tribal grantees.

Strongest source: “Emergency Rental Assistance: Treasury’s Oversight Is Limited by Incomplete Data and Risk Assessment,” GAO-23-105410, December 20, 2022, lines 276–280. [Direct source](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-105410)

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.9, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-009 — Pandemic-era learning losses were exceptionally large and unequal

The 2022 NAEP long-term-trend assessment found that nine-year-olds’ average reading score fell five points and mathematics fell seven points from 2020. It was the largest reading decline since 1990 and the first recorded mathematics decline. Scores fell at all measured achievement percentiles, with lower-performing students generally losing more than higher-performing students.

This is strong outcome evidence that children entered or remained in 2022 with significantly worse educational life chances. Attribution to Biden is weak: the losses span the pandemic, most school-opening and instructional decisions were state or local, and the federal government supplied substantial relief funds rather than directly operating schools. The administration nevertheless had responsibility for federal guidance, monitoring, and effective use of American Rescue Plan education funds.

Strongest source: “NAEP Long-Term Trend Assessment Results: Reading and Mathematics,” National Center for Education Statistics, 2022, lines 101–109 and 140. [Direct source](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/highlights/ltt/2022/)

Contrary or limiting evidence: The assessment identifies the deterioration but does not estimate how much federal relief mitigated it or isolate school closures from illness, family disruption, remote instruction, and other pandemic effects.

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-010 — Mortality improved as the acute pandemic burden receded, but major disparities remained

CDC estimated that the age-adjusted death rate declined 5.3% between 2021 and 2022. COVID-associated deaths fell 47%, from approximately 462,193 to 244,986, and life expectancy later was estimated to have risen from 76.4 to 77.5 years. Mortality nevertheless remained markedly higher among Black and American Indian/Alaska Native people, and COVID-associated mortality increased among children under 15.

The improvement is consistent with widespread vaccine availability, better treatment, prior immunity, federal distribution, and administration policy, but it cannot be causally assigned to Biden alone. Viral evolution, state policy, individual behavior, private health systems, and the inherited vaccine platform were central.

Strongest source: “Provisional Mortality Data—United States, 2022,” CDC/NCHS, MMWR, May 5, 2023, lines 68–92. [Direct source](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7218a3.htm)

Caution: The cited release used provisional data. Later final estimates confirm the broad life-expectancy recovery but do not solve causal attribution.

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-011 — Vaccine programs used equity targeting but did not eliminate racial disparities

GAO found that CDC, HRSA, and FEMA used racial and ethnic population data to select vaccination sites, provided translation and community outreach, extended clinic hours, and used pop-up clinics. CDC’s retail-pharmacy program exceeded its goal of delivering at least 40% of doses to groups other than non-Hispanic White people.

Available comparisons nevertheless suggested that some groups remained underrepresented: non-Hispanic Black people were roughly 12% of the population but about 9% of recipients with known race/ethnicity in the retail-pharmacy data. Missing race and ethnicity data might explain some or all of the measured difference.

The programs began under Biden in February 2021 and remained relevant to 2022 administration. They provide evidence of equity-oriented design and measurement but only limited evidence of equal realized uptake.

Strongest source: “COVID-19: Federal Efforts to Provide Vaccines to Racial and Ethnic Groups,” GAO-22-105079, February 7, 2022, lines 264–281 and report highlights. [Direct source](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105079)

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8.

### WEB-6B-012 — Maternal mortality declined but remained extremely unequal

CDC’s final 2022 vital statistics recorded 817 maternal deaths and a maternal mortality rate of 22.3 per 100,000 live births, down from 32.9 in 2021. Rates declined significantly for Black, White, and Hispanic women, but the Black maternal mortality rate remained 49.5—more than twice the White rate of 19.0 and nearly three times the Hispanic rate of 16.9.

The decline is favorable target-year evidence, while the racial disparity is strong contrary evidence about equality and dignity. The source does not establish that federal policy produced the change. Pandemic intensity, state maternity systems, Medicaid policy, hospital practice, demographic composition, and death-certificate classification all complicate attribution.

Strongest source: “Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2022,” CDC/NCHS, May 2, 2024, lines 49–53 and figures 1–3. [Direct source](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/hestat/maternal-mortality/2022/maternal-mortality-rates-2022.htm)

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.8, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-013 — The infant-formula crisis exposed regulatory and supply-chain weakness, followed by emergency relief and institutional correction

In February 2022, Abbott closed a major formula plant after contamination findings and a recall, worsening pandemic-related supply constraints. GAO later estimated that more than one-third of parents with infants were affected. The federal response included temporary authorization of foreign formula, WIC waivers allowing alternate brands and sizes, and the Access to Baby Formula Act, which permanently authorized USDA to waive program restrictions during future shortages and required WIC contracts to contain recall remedies.

The response helped restore access and created durable emergency authority, but later HHS OIG findings concluded that FDA lacked adequate policies and procedures for identifying formula risks and responding effectively through complaint, inspection, and recall processes. The plant failure was private, but FDA preparedness and response were within executive authority.

Strongest source: “WIC Infant Formula: Single-Supplier Competitive Contracts Reduce Program Costs and Modestly Increase Retail Prices,” GAO-25-106503, December 2024, lines 220–242. [Direct retrospective report](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-106503/index.html)

Period status: later retrospective evidence about a 2022 crisis. Attribution is moderate and mixed: the administration is connected both to the regulatory deficiencies and to the emergency response; Congress enacted the statutory remedy.

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.9, 6B.10.

### WEB-6B-014 — Homelessness and shelter capacity remained substantial

HUD’s January 2022 point-in-time count estimated 582,462 people experiencing homelessness on one night. The national inventory included approximately 1.046 million year-round homelessness-service beds, but only about 418,642 were shelter or transitional beds for people currently homeless—approximately 160,000 fewer than the PIT population.

This establishes a serious unmet housing baseline despite emergency rental aid and permanent-housing programs. The PIT count is not a direct measure of Biden’s causal effect: homelessness reflects long-running housing shortages, rents, local land-use rules, state and local systems, and pandemic interventions. Pandemic-era counting disruptions also make year-to-year comparisons hazardous.

Strongest source: “The 2022 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report to Congress, Part 1,” HUD/Abt Associates, accepted December 2022 and posted January 31, 2023, national inventory summary. [Report landing page](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/publications/2022-ahar-part-1-pit-estimates-of-homelessness.html)

Lenses: 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.10.

## Cross-lens synthesis without scoring

Well-evidenced lenses are 6B.2, 6B.3, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.9, and 6B.10. The record shows genuine federal welfare priority and several concrete administrative or statutory actions, especially health coverage, veterans’ protection, rental assistance, water infrastructure, vaccine equity, and future prescription-drug affordability.

The most consequential contrary evidence concerns failure to sustain the expanded Child Tax Credit, rising food insecurity, severe medical affordability, educational losses, persistent racial health disparities, homelessness, and the infant-formula regulatory failure. These are not all properly attributable to Biden, but they prevent treating federal program announcements as a proxy for broadly improved 2022 life chances.

Evidence for 6B.4 is mixed: CMS, VA, EPA, CDC, and Treasury demonstrate professional administration and measurement, while ERA oversight and FDA formula preparedness show important weaknesses. Evidence for 6B.7 is comparatively thin. No credible evidence found in this research showed systematic partisan conditioning of federal welfare benefits, but absence of evidence is not affirmative proof that no local political conditionality occurred.

Institutional durability is strongest for the IRA, PACT Act, drinking-water appropriations, Access to Baby Formula Act, and administrative data systems. The CTC experience points in the opposite direction: an intervention with unusually clear poverty effects expired after one year.

## Opened corroboration

- CMS’s detailed 2022 open-enrollment report corroborates the 14.5 million Marketplace total and 21% year-over-year increase.
- EPA’s 2022 anniversary materials corroborate the first 20 lead-service-line capitalization grants and equity-allocation planning.
- VA’s 2023 PACT dashboard provides later implementation counts.
- CDC final mortality publications corroborate the life-expectancy increase after the provisional MMWR.
- Census’s 2022 CTC working paper found that the 2021 expansion lifted approximately 2.1 million children above poverty, strengthening the policy-mechanism evidence but concerning the prior year.

## Uninspected or incompletely inspected leads

- State-level Medicaid, maternal-health, water, rental-aid, and education spending records could clarify federal versus state implementation.
- Treasury ERA recipient microdata could better identify racial, disability, and geographic distribution.
- Department of Education state plans and ESSER expenditure data could test whether relief funds reached high-poverty districts and improved recovery.
- CDC’s 2022 child vaccination-disparity study and AdultVaxView survey could add vaccine-specific subgroup detail.
- Independent evaluations of lead-line replacement and PACT implementation would strengthen outcome and durability assessment.
- Abortion access after *Dobbs* is material to women’s health and dignity, but a careful federal/state authority analysis was not completed here.
- Disability services, long-term care, childcare availability, rural access, tribal service delivery, and water/sanitation outcomes remain underdeveloped.

## Rejected or non-evidentiary materials

- White House fact sheets were not used as principal evidence where agency data, GAO, Census, or statutory implementation documents were available; they are advocacy-oriented and often combine announcements with projected benefits.
- The client matrix and any prior score were excluded as evidence.
- News articles repeating agency figures without additional investigation were excluded as duplicative.
- Broad UNDP/WDI country-level priors were not used to determine direction because they are insufficiently discriminating for one U.S. calendar year and weakly attributable to Biden.
- Later program totals were not treated as 2022 outcomes; where useful, they are explicitly marked as retrospective implementation evidence.

## Remaining uncertainty and research saturation

Further work is likely to add material information mainly through subnational and distributional analysis—not more national announcements. The largest gaps are education-relief effectiveness, disability and long-term-care access, childcare, tribal/rural outcomes, post-*Dobbs* reproductive access, and state-level delivery. Additional general web searching is otherwise likely to repeat the national facts above.

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"The State of U.S. Health Insurance in 2022","publisher":"Commonwealth Fund","publication_date":"2022-09-29","url":"https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/issue-briefs/2022/sep/state-us-health-insurance-2022-biennial-survey","claim":"In a 2022 survey, 46% of working-age adults reported delaying or skipping care because of cost, 42% had medical-bill or debt problems, and inability to pay an unexpected $1,000 bill was especially prevalent among low-income, Black, and Hispanic adults.","locator":"lines 150-155, 196-197, 255","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-004","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_healthcare_affordability_underinsurance","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10"],"source_type":"independent_household_survey","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Established independent health-policy survey with transparent methods, but self-reported responses and sampling uncertainty apply.","final_evidence_use":"Contrary evidence limiting the practical meaning of insurance-coverage gains.","period_fit":"Direct 2022 survey evidence.","ruler_attribution":"Low; reflects long-standing health-system structure and multiple public and private payers.","contrary_evidence":"Coverage rates reached historic highs and enhanced Marketplace subsidies reduced premiums for many enrollees.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Reduced Drug Prices, Enhanced Medicare Benefits Under the Inflation Reduction Act: Frequently Asked Questions","publisher":"Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services","publication_date":"2022-10-05","url":"https://www.cms.gov/files/document/10522-external-faqs-about-inflation-reduction-act.pdf","claim":"The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act created Medicare insulin, vaccine, catastrophic-cost, low-income-subsidy, inflation-rebate, and drug-negotiation reforms, with most beneficiary savings beginning in 2023-2025.","locator":"pp. 1-2, lines 18-55","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-005","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_ira_medicare_drug_affordability_institutions","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.9","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_statutory_implementation_document","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"CMS accurately describes enacted statutory requirements and implementation dates.","final_evidence_use":"Strong durable-institution evidence, not a realized 2022 outcome.","period_fit":"Law enacted and implementation begun in 2022; most delivery occurred later.","ruler_attribution":"Strong but shared with Congress; Biden advocated for and signed the law and directed executive implementation.","contrary_evidence":"Most savings had not begun in 2022, and the insulin cap did not cover all privately insured or uninsured patients.","lenses":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.9","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"VA opens health care eligibility for Vietnam, Gulf War, post-9/11 Veterans under PACT Act","publisher":"U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs","publication_date":"2022-09-28","url":"https://news.va.gov/press-room/va-opens-health-care-eligibility-for-vietnam-gulf-war-post-9-11-veterans-under-pact-act/","claim":"The PACT Act, signed August 10, 2022, expanded VA health-care eligibility beginning October 1 for specified toxic-exposed veterans and established presumptions, screenings, research, and administrative capacity.","locator":"lines 62-73","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-006","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_pact_act_toxic_exposed_veterans","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_program_and_legal_record","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"VA implementation notice describing enacted eligibility and dates; later VA dashboard corroborates uptake.","final_evidence_use":"Vulnerable-group access, dignity, and durable entitlement evidence.","period_fit":"Enacted and initial eligibility implemented in 2022; most uptake later.","ruler_attribution":"Strong but shared with bipartisan Congress and long-running veterans advocacy.","contrary_evidence":"Initial health outcomes were not measurable in 2022, and later administrative capacity determined realized access.","lenses":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Bipartisan Infrastructure Law: EPA’s Year One Anniversary Report","publisher":"U.S. Environmental Protection Agency","publication_date":"2022-11","url":"https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-11/V-4_BIL_FirstAnniversaryReport_Nov142022.pdf","claim":"By November 1, 2022 EPA reported about $4.24 billion in water-program obligations, including roughly $1.17 billion each for lead-service-line replacement and general drinking-water revolving funds, and initial state capitalization grants.","locator":"funding table and first-year accomplishments","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-007","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_water_infrastructure_lead_funding_obligations","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9"],"source_type":"official_administrative_financial_report","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Specific obligation data from the administering agency, but self-reported and not evidence of completed replacements or health outcomes.","final_evidence_use":"Implementation and institutional investment in safe water, with delivery caveat.","period_fit":"Direct FY2022 appropriation and obligation activity.","ruler_attribution":"Moderate-to-strong for advocacy, signature, and EPA execution; shared with Congress, states, and utilities.","contrary_evidence":"Obligated funds do not demonstrate completed pipes, equitable receipt, or target-year health gains.","lenses":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Emergency Rental Assistance: Treasury's Oversight Is Limited by Incomplete Data and Risk Assessment","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2022-12-20","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-105410","claim":"ERA likely limited evictions and reached very-low-income renters, but delivery was initially slow, recipient data were incomplete, risk controls were weak, and $3.1 billion in 2022 reallocations did not consistently align funding with renter need and grantee capacity.","locator":"lines 276-280 and report highlights","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-008","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_emergency_rental_assistance_delivery_oversight","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10"],"source_type":"independent_government_audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO audit combines Treasury data, documentation, grantee interviews, and explicit limitations.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed crisis-protection evidence: meaningful assistance alongside management and equity weaknesses.","period_fit":"Program activity and reallocation through October 2022, with earlier implementation history.","ruler_attribution":"Moderate; ERA1 was inherited, ERA2 was Biden-era legislation, Treasury administered both, and local grantees controlled household delivery.","contrary_evidence":"Third-party eviction evidence indicates substantial protection, and administrative flexibility accelerated payments.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"NAEP Long-Term Trend Assessment Results: Reading and Mathematics","publisher":"National Center for Education Statistics","publication_date":"2022","url":"https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/highlights/ltt/2022/","claim":"Nine-year-olds' reading scores fell five points and mathematics scores seven points from 2020 to 2022, the largest reading decline since 1990 and first mathematics decline, with generally larger losses among lower-performing students.","locator":"lines 101-109 and 140","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-009","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_pandemic_learning_loss_naep","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_representative_assessment","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"NCES nationally representative standardized assessment with historical comparability.","final_evidence_use":"Major adverse education and unequal-life-chances outcome.","period_fit":"Direct winter-2022 assessment compared with winter 2020.","ruler_attribution":"Low; losses span the pandemic and education is primarily state/local, though federal relief monitoring was an executive responsibility.","contrary_evidence":"Federal relief may have mitigated losses, but this assessment does not estimate its effect.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Provisional Mortality Data—United States, 2022","publisher":"CDC National Center for Health Statistics","publication_date":"2023-05-05","url":"https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7218a3.htm","claim":"The age-adjusted death rate fell 5.3% in 2022 and COVID-associated deaths fell 47%, but Black and American Indian/Alaska Native mortality remained disproportionately high and child COVID mortality rates increased.","locator":"lines 68-92","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-010","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_mortality_covid_decline_disparities","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_vital_statistics","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"National death-certificate surveillance with explicit provisional-data and classification caveats; broad trend later corroborated by final data.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable crisis trajectory qualified by persistent inequality and weak causal attribution.","period_fit":"Direct calendar-year 2022 mortality.","ruler_attribution":"Low-to-moderate; federal vaccines, treatments, and distribution contributed, but viral evolution, immunity, states, providers, and behavior were also decisive.","contrary_evidence":"COVID still caused approximately 245,000 associated deaths, disparities remained large, and mortality rose among some child age groups.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"COVID-19: Federal Efforts to Provide Vaccines to Racial and Ethnic Groups","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2022-02-07","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105079","claim":"CDC, HRSA, and FEMA used population data, translation, extended hours, outreach, and pop-up clinics to target underserved groups; CDC exceeded its aggregate diversity goal, but available comparisons suggested continuing underrepresentation of some groups, including Black recipients.","locator":"lines 264-281 and report highlights","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-011","canonical_fact_key":"usa_biden_vaccine_equity_programs_disparities","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8"],"source_type":"independent_government_audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO reviewed agency data and documentation and interviewed state and stakeholder officials, while explicitly identifying missing demographic data.","final_evidence_use":"Equity-oriented implementation and measurement evidence, qualified by incomplete realization.","period_fit":"Published in 2022 using program data through September 2021; inherited context for 2022 operations.","ruler_attribution":"Strong for program launch and federal design under Biden; outcomes also depended on states, pharmacies, providers, and uptake.","contrary_evidence":"Missing race and ethnicity data could explain some or all measured disparities, and aggregate targets can mask subgroup shortfalls.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2022","publisher":"CDC National Center for Health Statistics","publication_date":"2024-05-02","url":"https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/hestat/maternal-mortality/2022/maternal-mortality-rates-2022.htm","claim":"Maternal mortality declined from 32.9 per 100,000 live births in 2021 to 22.3 in 2022, but the Black maternal mortality rate remained 49.5 versus 19.0 for White women and 16.9 for Hispanic women.","locator":"lines 49-53 and figures 1-3","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-012","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_maternal_mortality_decline_racial_gap","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_final_vital_statistics","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Final national vital-statistics files with stated ICD definitions and significance testing.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable health trajectory with severe persistent racial inequality.","period_fit":"Direct calendar-year 2022 outcome, published retrospectively.","ruler_attribution":"Low; no causal analysis links the annual change to federal policy, and state and provider systems are central.","contrary_evidence":"Rates remained above 2018-2020 levels and Black women faced more than twice the White rate.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"WIC Infant Formula: Single-Supplier Competitive Contracts Reduce Program Costs and Modestly Increase Retail Prices","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2024-12","url":"https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-106503/index.html","claim":"The 2022 formula shortage affected more than one-third of parents with infants; federal agencies authorized imports and WIC substitutions, and the Access to Baby Formula Act created durable waiver and contract-remedy authority, while later HHS OIG work found inadequate FDA risk-identification and response procedures.","locator":"lines 220-242","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-013","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_infant_formula_shortage_response_regulatory_failure","disposition":"fully_extracted_later_retrospective","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.9","6B.10"],"source_type":"independent_government_retrospective_audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO synthesizes federal actions, later inspector-general findings, legislation, and survey estimates, though published two years later.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed crisis-management and institutional-correction evidence.","period_fit":"Later retrospective report about a direct 2022 crisis and response.","ruler_attribution":"Moderate and mixed: FDA preparedness and emergency administration were executive responsibilities; plant closure was private and Congress enacted statutory remedies.","contrary_evidence":"Federal waivers, imports, and legislation expanded supply and future resilience, but they followed a serious preventable oversight and concentration failure.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.9","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"The 2022 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report to Congress: Part 1","publisher":"U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development / Abt Associates","publication_date":"2023-01-31","url":"https://www.huduser.gov/portal/publications/2022-ahar-part-1-pit-estimates-of-homelessness.html","claim":"HUD estimated 582,462 people experienced homelessness on one night in January 2022, while the inventory of beds for people currently homeless was approximately 160,000 below that count.","locator":"national PIT and housing-inventory summary; report accepted December 2022","provisional_id":"WEB-6B-014","canonical_fact_key":"usa_2022_homelessness_shelter_capacity_gap","disposition":"fully_extracted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"],"source_type":"official_point_in_time_administrative_estimate","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Standard national HUD count and inventory, but PIT methods undercount unsheltered people and pandemic disruptions impair longitudinal comparison.","final_evidence_use":"Unmet housing-need baseline and contrary access evidence.","period_fit":"Direct January 2022 snapshot.","ruler_attribution":"Low; homelessness reflects long-term housing supply, rents, local land-use policy, state systems, and federal programs across administrations.","contrary_evidence":"Emergency rental assistance and permanent-housing inventory mitigated homelessness, and one-night counts do not measure all annual homelessness or policy effects.","lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.6","6B.8","6B.10"]}
